The '''National Survey of Family Growth''' ('''NSFG''') is a [[Opinion poll|survey]] conducted by the [[National Center for Health Statistics]] division of the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] to understand trends related to fertility, family structure, and demographics in the United States.<ref name=official>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg.htm|title = National Survey of Family Growth|publisher = [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]]|accessdate = April 22, 2014}}</ref>

==History and details==

The National Survey of Family Growth is conducted in five-year cycles. In each cycle, surveys are administered via personal interviews with people at homes. The interviewees generally comprise only the civilian, non-institutionalized population.<ref name="about">{{cite web |title=About the National Survey of Family Growth |url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/about_nsfg.htm |accessdate=2024-01-07 |publisher=National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>

The cycles so far have been:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_questionnaires.htm|title = Questionnaires, Datasets, and Related Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014}}</ref>

* Cycle 1, started 1973<ref name=cycle1>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_cycle1.htm|title = NSFG - Cycle 1 (1973): Public Use Data Files, Codebooks, and Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>
* Cycle 2, started 1976<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_cycle2.htm|title = NSFG - Cycle 2 (1976): Public Use Data Files, Codebooks, and Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>
* Cycle 3, started 1982<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_cycle3.htm|title = NSFG - Cycle 3 (1982): Public Use Data Files, Codebooks, and Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>
* Cycle 4, started 1988<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_cycle4.htm|title = NSFG - Cycle 4 (1988): Public Use Data Files, Codebooks, and Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>
* Cycle 5, started 1995<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_cycle5.htm|title = NSFG - Cycle 5 (1995): Public Use Data Files, Codebooks, and Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>
* Cycle 6, started 2002<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_cycle6.htm|title = NSFG - Cycle 6 (2002): Public Use Data Files, Codebooks, and Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>
* 2006–2010 NSFG<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_2006_2010_puf.htm|title = 2006-2010 NSFG: Public Use Data Files, Codebooks, and Documentation|accessdate = April 22, 2014|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth}}</ref>
* 2011–2013 NSFG<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2019-03-04|title=NSFG - About the National Survey of Family Growth|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/about_nsfg.htm|access-date=2020-08-05|website=www.cdc.gov|language=en-us}}</ref>
* 2013–2015 NSFG<ref name=":0" />
* 2015–2019 NSFG<ref name=":0" />

While Cycles 1–5 surveyed only women, Cycle 6 and later surveyed both men and women and used households as the unit of analysis. Cycle 6 surveyed 12,571 respondents 15–44 years of age: 7,643 females and 4,928 males. The 2006–2010 NSFG surveyed 22,682 interviews: over 10,000 interviews with men and more than 12,000 interviews with women.<ref name=about/> In 2006, the NSFG shifted from periodic surveys to continuous interviewing.<ref name=":0" /> For Cycle 6 onward, the surveys were conducted in person by female interviewers who are hired and managed by the [[University of Michigan Institute for Social Research]].<ref name=about/> The survey samples are intended to be nationally representative but not necessarily representative at subnational levels (such as individual states, ethnicities, or religions).<ref name=about/>

NSFG resumed data collection in January 2022 with a multi-mode, continuous survey design. Under this survey design, data collection will continue through December 2029.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-16 |title=NSFG - About the National Survey of Family Growth |url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/about_nsfg.htm |access-date=2025-05-02 |website=www.cdc.gov |language=en-us}}</ref>

==Data==

For the survey cycles that have been completed, data is available both in the form of [[portable document format]] summaries and as full data files. In addition, program statements are available in SAS, SPSS, and STATA.<ref name=cycle1/>

Key statistics are also browsable online.<ref name=statistics>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/key_statistics.htm|title = NSFG - Key Statistics|publisher = National Survey of Family Growth|accessdate = April 22, 2014}}</ref>

NSFG data is also mirrored on the website of the [[University of Michigan]]'s [[Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.icpsr.umich.edu/icpsrweb/ICPSR/series/48|title = National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG) Series|publisher = [[Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research]], [[University of Michigan]]|accessdate = April 22, 2014}}</ref>

==Reception and impact==

===Claims===

Data collected by the NSFG are used as follows:<ref name=about/>

* By scholars in the [[behavioral science]]s (e.g., [[sociology]], [[demography]], and [[economics]]) to study [[marriage]], [[divorce]], [[fertility]], and [[family]] life
* By scholars in public health to study reproductive, maternal and infant health topics
* By agencies of the US [[Department of Health and Human Services]], to brief senior officials and to inform program decision-making in research programs and in health and social service programs
* By state and local governments to plan health and social service programs
* By private-sector research organizations which distribute the information to the public and to policy makers
* By the press, to prepare articles on a number of topics related to health and family life

===Academic research===

The NSFG has been cited in more than 1,300 journal articles, NHCS reports, and book chapters.<ref name=about/> Research citing the NSFG is concentrated on topics related to family planning, contraception, abortion, and fertility.<ref>{{cite journal|title = Estimates of contraceptive failure from the 2002 National Survey of Family Growth|last1 = Kost|first1 = Kathryn|last2 = Singh|first2 = Susheela|last3 = Vaughan|first3 = Barbara|last4 = Trussell|first4 = James|last5 = Bankole|first5 = Akinrinola|journal = [[Contraception (journal)|Contraception]]|volume = 77|issue = 1|pages = 10–21|date = January 2008|doi = 10.1016/j.contraception.2007.09.013|pmid=18082661|pmc=2811396}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.guttmacher.org/pubs/journals/3124699.html|title = Are All Contraceptive Failures Unintended Pregnancies? Evidence from the 1995 National Survey of Family Growth|last1= Trussell|first1 = James|last2 = Vaughan|first2 = Barbara|last3 = Stanford|first3 = Joseph|journal = [[Family Planning Perspectives]]|volume = 31|issue = 5|date = September–October 1999|accessdate = April 22, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.guttmacher.org/pubs/journals/3012898.html|title = Measuring the Extent of Abortion Underreporting In the 1995 National Survey of Family Growth|journal = [[Family Planning Perspectives]]|volume = 30|issue = 3|date = May–June 1998|accessdate = April 22, 2014|last1 = Fu|first1 = Haishan|last2 = Darroch|first2 = Jacqueline E.|last3 = Henshaw|first3 = Stanley K.|last4 = Kolb|first4 = Elizabeth| pages=128–33, 138 | doi=10.2307/2991627 | jstor=2991627 | pmid=9635261 |url-access = subscription}}</ref>
